summary:
Private adult consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful in Fiji since 1 February 2010, when the Crimes Decree 2009, cited as the Crimes Act 2010, took effect and repealed the historic Penal Code offence under Article 175. That offence had carried a maximum penalty of fourteen years imprisonment.

In April 2005 two men, Australian tourist Thomas McCosker and Fijian man Dhirendra Nadan, received two-year prison sentences under Article 175 for consensual sex. The trial judge described the acts as so disgusting that any decent person would vomit. Human Rights Watch called for the charges to be dropped and the men released, citing the 1997 constitutional prohibition on sexual orientation discrimination. The convictions were overturned in August 2005 by the highest court as a violation of the Constitution.

Enforcement ended in practice before repeal. In July 2006 the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.

Fiji prohibited sexual orientation discrimination in its 1997 Constitution, the second such constitutional protection in the world after South Africa. That Constitution was abolished in 2009. The Constitution promulgated in September 2013 reinstated the protection and extended it. Article 26(3)(a) bans unfair direct or indirect discrimination on grounds including sex, gender, gender identity and expression and sexual orientation. In 2013 the Government also included sexual orientation and gender identity in anti-hate speech law and in law dealing with discrimination in certain businesses.

No legal route exists for a trans person to change a gender marker. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, despite the constitutional protection on gender identity and expression. A 2023 Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study on legal gender recognition describes this as constitutional protection with zero implementation, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.

Fiji recognises a traditional third-gender population known as vaka sa lewa lewa, people assigned male at birth who dress, act and behave as female. Sources describe this group as traditionally accepted by Fijian society. That acceptance has no legal effect.

Fiji provides no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions. The Marriage Act 2002 limits marriage to one man and one woman, with an express ban on same-sex marriage since 2002. Prime ministerial opposition was reaffirmed on 26 March 2013, in January 2016 and in 2019.

Lack of trust in police due to possible harassment likely discourages LGBTQ people from reporting anti-gay violence or hateful discrimination. Reports describe hate crimes as rare. Documented cases include the brutal murder in Suva on 1 July 2001 of Red Cross leader John Maurice Scott and his partner Gregory Scrivener in an apparent homophobic attack with a possible political motive, the brutal murder in Suva in May 2018 of a young transgender woman, and a gay student found dead in Nasinu in September 2017. Activists report that physical violence and domestic abuse operate as familial conversion therapy for many LGBTQ+ people.

Reports of societal discrimination and bullying are described as not uncommon. Social mores regarding sexual orientation and gender identity are described as conservative, with little public support for LGBTQ rights. Majority Methodist and Catholic denominations traditionally view transgender identities negatively. The Muslim minority, about 6% of the population, tends to view cross-dressing as sinful behavior that needs to be fixed. In April 2005 Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex and called homosexuality a sin in a conservative Christian nation, days after the two-year sentences noted above.

Public displays of affection are not illegal. Visitors are advised that such displays are generally considered offensive.

The Government has in the past cancelled gay pride marches. LGBTQ activists organised activities on 17 May 2013 for the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia, held an event in Suva in 2017 attended by activists and religious figures, and held Fiji's first pride parade on 17 May 2018 in Lautoka with local police escort and an address by former President Epeli Nailatikau.
tangentialFactors:
Fiji underwent constitutional interruption in the period relevant to decriminalisation. A state of emergency followed the ousting of the Prime Minister in 2007, and the 1997 Constitution was abolished in 2009 before the 2010 Crimes Decree and the 2013 Constitution.

During criminalisation, the New Zealand AIDS Foundation linked the sodomy law to public health harm. Its executive director Rachael Le Mesurier said criminalisation drove sex underground and contributed to HIV spread.

Sources contrast longstanding cultural acceptance of vaka sa lewa lewa with current opposition from prevailing Christian and Muslim mores. That contrast is presented as explanation for the gap between traditional acceptance and lack of legal recognition.
localsOnly:
Discrimination in employment based on sexual orientation is banned under the Employment Relations Promulgation 2007. Workplace protections on sexual orientation have therefore applied since 2007.

Registered mental health professionals are barred from attempting to change sexual orientation. The Mental Health Decree 2010 provides that a person is not mentally ill if the person refuses or fails to express a particular sexual orientation, and prohibits conversion practices by registered professionals.

In April 2017 the Ministry of Health confirmed that gay and bisexual men are banned from donating blood, after a gay man was refused donation because of his sexual orientation.

An Outright International overview updated 12 March 2026 states that organisations cannot register and that intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected. No same-sex marriage route and no legal gender recognition route apply to residents.

In 2022 the National Federation Party endorsed Divina Loloma, a transgender woman, as the first openly LGBTQ candidate ever endorsed by a political party. All People's Party leader Tuiloma Tawaivuna criticised the nomination, calling transgender people an abomination and Biblically wrong.
outOfScopeNotes:
One source flag in the Outright International overview marks same-sex relations as illegal, which is unresolved against the same overview and all other sources recording decriminalisation since 2010. The flag was not relied on for the assessment above.

No sourced provision on visitor entry, visa sex-marker rules, airport or other screening that risks outing, bathroom or facilities law, or access to gender-affirming care in Fiji was found in the inventory. Those points are not sourced here.

No sourced national hate-crime penalty provision distinct from the 2013 hate-speech and business-discrimination protections was found in the inventory.
